triage.name: Heart Failure
triage.reason: Common syndrome with classic dyspnea, edema and orthopnea history, exam findings, and a clear workup including BNP and echocardiography; rich differential.

demographics: Men tend to develop it at a younger age than women
More common and more severe at younger ages in African American patients

risk_factors.text: Coronary artery disease or prior myocardial infarction
Family history of heart failure or cardiomyopathy
Prior chest radiation or cardiotoxic chemotherapy

family_history: Heart failure or cardiomyopathy in a first-degree relative
Sudden cardiac death in a young relative

chief_complaints.text: I get winded just walking to the mailbox
My ankles and feet are swollen
I can't lie flat at night — I have to prop myself up with pillows
I wake up in the middle of the night gasping for air
I'm tired all the time and have no energy
I've gained weight and my clothes feel tight

hpi.onset: Usually gradual over weeks to months; can be abrupt over hours to days after a myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, infection or valve rupture
hpi.duration: Weeks to months for chronic heart failure; hours to days for acute decompensation
hpi.progression: Exertional breathlessness appears first and slowly limits activity; orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema and weight gain follow as congestion builds
hpi.location: Breathlessness is felt in the chest; swelling is in the ankles, lower legs and sometimes the abdomen
hpi.quality: Air hunger and heaviness in the chest; swelling is pitting and painless
hpi.severity: Mild at first, then moderate to severe; patients often describe it as 4–8/10 when they finally seek care
hpi.timing: Worse with activity and when lying flat; better after sitting up or resting

associated_symptoms.text: Swelling of the ankles and lower legs
Waking at night short of breath
Dry cough, worse at night or lying down
Loss of appetite, early fullness, nausea
Abdominal bloating or right upper quadrant discomfort

pertinent_negatives: Pleuritic chest pain that worsens with deep breath
Sudden pleuritic chest pain with hemoptysis
Current use of NSAIDs or thiazolidinediones

negatives: Severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back

argues_against: Primary gastrointestinal bleeding or hepatobiliary disease
Urinary tract infection or renal colic

negatives: Panic attacks as the primary problem

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, falls, poor appetite or generalized weakness rather than classic dyspnea; exertional symptoms are often attributed to aging.
Breathlessness and leg swelling are blamed on weight; edema may be hard to see and BNP can be lower than expected.
Normal pregnancy causes mild dyspnea, leg swelling and fatigue, so worsening orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and a new murmur are the clues.
Volume overload from kidney disease can mimic heart failure; edema and dyspnea overlap and BNP is elevated by reduced clearance.
Autonomic neuropathy can blunt exertional symptoms, and patients may present later with silent ischemia or advanced congestion.

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, mild dyspnea only with exertion, no distress
general.moderate: Mild respiratory distress at rest, prefers sitting upright, speaks in full sentences
general.severe: Obvious respiratory distress, uses accessory muscles, speaks in short phrases, anxious
general.critical: Acutely dyspneic and diaphoretic, tripod positioning, unable to speak in full sentences, may be confused or agitated

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular vein with the patient at 45 degrees and measure the vertical height above the sternal angle
findings.finding: Jugular venous pressure elevated above 3–4 cm above the sternal angle

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the right upper quadrant for 10–15 seconds while watching the jugular venous pulsation
findings.finding: Sustained rise in jugular venous pressure that does not fall during abdominal pressure

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the apex with the bell while the patient lies in the left lateral position
findings.finding: Third heart sound (S3 gallop)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the apical impulse in the left lateral decubitus position
findings.finding: Apical impulse displaced laterally and inferiorly, sustained and enlarged

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all valve areas with the diaphragm and bell
findings.finding: Systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation at the apex or of aortic stenosis at the right upper sternal border

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the posterior lung bases with the diaphragm
findings.finding: Fine inspiratory crackles at the bases that do not clear with coughing
Dullness at the bases from pleural effusion

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the chest during quiet and forced expiration
findings.finding: Diffuse expiratory wheezing (cardiac asthma)

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the dorsum of the foot and the lower shin for several seconds
findings.finding: Bilateral pitting edema of the ankles and lower legs, often extending to the thighs when severe

findings.maneuver: Assess skin temperature and capillary refill at the hands and feet
findings.finding: Cool, pale extremities with prolonged capillary refill and mottling

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant below the costal margin
findings.finding: Tender, pulsatile hepatomegaly from hepatic congestion

findings.maneuver: Percuss the flanks for shifting dullness or perform a fluid wave
findings.finding: Ascites

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation, attention and level of consciousness
findings.finding: Confusion, somnolence or agitation from hypoperfusion or hypoxemia

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature and inspect for a source of infection
findings.finding: No fever and no obvious infectious source

findings.maneuver: Palpate both calves and compare circumference
findings.finding: No unilateral calf tenderness or swelling

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to take a deep breath and cough while auscultating
findings.finding: No pleuritic chest pain or pleural rub

labs.caveat: A normal BNP in an untreated patient makes heart failure unlikely; levels are lower in obesity and higher in renal impairment, older age and atrial fibrillation.
Alternative to BNP; age-stratified cutoffs are used, and levels rise with reduced kidney function.
Mildly elevated troponin is common in acute decompensation from demand ischemia; marked elevation suggests acute coronary syndrome as the trigger.
Cardiorenal syndrome; also guides diuretic dosing and safety of renin-angiotensin blockade.
Rises with reduced effective circulating volume and diuresis.
Dilutional hyponatremia from neurohormonal activation; a marker of worse prognosis.
Hypokalemia from loop diuretics; hyperkalemia can occur with renin-angiotensin blockade or renal failure.
Anemia can both cause and worsen heart failure; look for iron deficiency.
Both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism can precipitate or mimic heart failure.
Diabetes is a common driver of heart failure and affects management.
Low albumin from hepatic congestion, malnutrition or protein-losing states.
Mild elevation from hepatic congestion; marked elevation suggests a primary liver problem.
Congestive hepatopathy; usually mild and improves with decongestion.
Proteinuria may reflect the underlying cause (hypertensive or diabetic nephropathy) or renal congestion.
Elevated lactate with cool extremities and hypotension indicates cardiogenic shock.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation
Tachycardia
Left axis deviation
Left atrial enlargement (broad, notched P wave in lead II, terminal negative deflection in V1)
Low voltage in the limb leads
Left bundle branch block
Pathologic Q waves from prior myocardial infarction
Prolonged QT interval
ST depression or T wave inversion from demand ischemia or strain
ST elevation in a coronary distribution suggesting acute myocardial infarction as the trigger
Nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay
Voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy

imaging.preferred_when: All patients with suspected heart failure

findings.text: Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (HFrEF) or preserved ejection fraction with diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF)
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left atrial enlargement
Global or regional wall motion abnormality suggesting prior or acute infarction
Valvular disease, most often mitral regurgitation or aortic stenosis
Right ventricular dilation or dysfunction and elevated estimated pulmonary artery pressure
Pericardial effusion

imaging.preferred_when: Dyspnea of unclear cause; first-line in the emergency setting

findings.text: Cardiomegaly with increased cardiothoracic ratio
Pulmonary vascular congestion with cephalization of vessels
Bilateral pleural effusions, often larger on the right
Interstitial or alveolar edema with perihilar haziness
Kerley B lines
Normal chest x-ray despite clinical heart failure

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected coronary artery disease as the cause, or before surgical or device therapy

findings.text: Significant coronary artery stenosis
Multivessel or left main disease
No obstructive coronary disease (nonischemic cardiomyopathy)

imaging.preferred_when: Unclear cause of cardiomyopathy or suspected infiltrative or inflammatory disease

findings.text: Late gadolinium enhancement in a pattern suggesting infarction, myocarditis or infiltrative disease
Increased myocardial wall thickness suggesting amyloidosis or hypertrophy
Myocardial edema suggesting active inflammation

imaging.study: CT chest with IV contrast (CT pulmonary angiography)
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pulmonary embolism or when echocardiography is unavailable

findings.text: Filling defect in the pulmonary arteries (pulmonary embolism)
Right ventricular enlargement
Pleural effusions and pulmonary edema

imaging.preferred_when: Assessing for ischemia when exercise testing is not feasible

findings.text: Reversible perfusion defect indicating inducible ischemia
Fixed defect indicating prior infarction

initial.why: Supports the diagnosis and helps distinguish cardiac from pulmonary causes of dyspnea
Alternative natriuretic peptide; useful when BNP is unavailable
Looks for anemia or infection as a trigger
Assesses renal function, electrolytes and sodium before diuresis
Defines ejection fraction, wall motion, valves and chamber size
Shows cardiomegaly, congestion and effusions; helps exclude pneumonia
Detects arrhythmia, ischemia, hypertrophy or conduction disease
Screens for acute coronary syndrome as the precipitant
initial.only_if: chest pain, ischemic ECG changes or hemodynamic instability

initial.why: Thyroid disease can cause or worsen heart failure
Identifies diabetes as a contributing cause
Assesses perfusion in suspected cardiogenic shock
initial.only_if: hypotension, cool extremities or altered mental status

supporting.why: Assesses hepatic congestion and nutritional status
Screens for proteinuria suggesting a renal contribution
Cardiovascular risk assessment and statin decisions
Iron deficiency is common and treatable in heart failure

supporting.only_if: angina, ischemic ECG changes or high pretest probability of coronary disease

supporting.why: Clarifies the cause when echocardiography is inconclusive
supporting.only_if: cause remains unclear or infiltrative disease is suspected

supporting.test: CT chest with IV contrast (CT pulmonary angiography)
supporting.only_if: sudden worsening dyspnea with risk factors or pleuritic pain

not_indicated.why: Nonspecific in heart failure and rarely changes management
Not needed unless infection is suspected
No role in heart failure workup
Reserved for severe hypoxemia or suspected hypercapnia
not_indicated.only_if: severe respiratory distress or suspected CO2 retention

not_indicated.test: CT chest with IV contrast (CT pulmonary angiography)
not_indicated.why: Only when pulmonary embolism is suspected

decision_points: Check BNP or NT-proBNP before echocardiography to support the diagnosis when the cause of dyspnea is unclear
Echocardiography is required to classify HFrEF versus HFpEF and guide therapy
Troponin and ECG should be obtained urgently when acute coronary syndrome is suspected as the trigger
Assess for cardiogenic shock (hypotension, cool extremities, elevated lactate) and escalate care accordingly
Evaluate for reversible precipitants such as infection, arrhythmia, ischemia, nonadherence and NSAID use

criteria.name: Framingham criteria for heart failure
criteria.summary: Combines major and minor clinical features; two major or one major plus two minor features support the diagnosis.
items: Major: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, neck vein distention, rales, cardiomegaly, acute pulmonary edema, S3 gallop, increased venous pressure, hepatomegaly, weight loss with treatment
Minor: ankle edema, night cough, dyspnea on exertion, hepatomegaly, pleural effusion, tachycardia, weight loss with treatment

differential.name: COPD exacerbation
differential.why_considered: Dyspnea, wheezing, cough and reduced exercise tolerance in an older smoker overlap heavily with heart failure.

history: Long-standing smoking history with chronic productive cough
Symptoms worse with respiratory infections, better with inhalers
Less orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
exam: Barrel chest, prolonged expiration, diffuse wheezing
No elevated jugular venous pressure or S3 gallop
Edema is usually absent or mild
labs: BNP normal or only mildly elevated
Eosinophilia or elevated carbon dioxide on blood gas
imaging: Hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms and increased retrosternal air space on chest x-ray
No pulmonary vascular congestion or cardiomegaly

differential.name: Pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Fever, cough, dyspnea and crackles can mimic acute heart failure with pulmonary congestion.
differential.trigger: Fever, productive cough or focal lung findings

history: Acute fever with chills and productive purulent sputum
Pleuritic chest pain
No orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
exam: Focal crackles, dullness or bronchial breath sounds
No elevated jugular venous pressure or S3 gallop
labs: BNP usually normal or only mildly elevated
imaging: Lobar or segmental consolidation on chest x-ray

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Sudden dyspnea, tachycardia and hypoxemia can resemble acute decompensated heart failure.
differential.trigger: Sudden onset dyspnea with pleuritic pain, hemoptysis or unilateral leg swelling

history: Abrupt onset over minutes to hours
Pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis or syncope
Recent immobilization, surgery or long travel
exam: Tachycardia and hypoxemia with clear lungs
No orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
imaging: Filling defect in pulmonary arteries on CT pulmonary angiography
Right ventricular enlargement without left-sided congestion
ecg: Sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3 pattern or right axis deviation

differential.name: Nephrotic syndrome
differential.why_considered: Generalized edema, weight gain and dyspnea from fluid overload can look like right-sided heart failure.

history: Frothy urine and periorbital edema
Recent infection or new medication
No orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
exam: No elevated jugular venous pressure or S3 gallop
imaging: Normal heart size and no pulmonary congestion on chest x-ray

differential.name: Cirrhosis with ascites
differential.why_considered: Abdominal swelling, leg edema and dyspnea from ascites can mimic right-sided heart failure.

history: Known liver disease, alcohol use or hepatitis
Jaundice, easy bruising and confusion
No orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
exam: Spider angiomata, palmar erythema and caput medusae
Ascites with a small, nonpulsatile liver
imaging: Nodular liver with portal hypertension and splenomegaly on ultrasound

differential.name: Severe anemia
differential.why_considered: Exertional dyspnea, fatigue, tachycardia and edema from high-output state can resemble heart failure.

history: Pallor, pica or bleeding
No orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
exam: Flow murmur without elevated jugular venous pressure or S3
imaging: Normal cardiac chambers and no congestion on echocardiography

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, edema and dyspnea on exertion overlap with heart failure.

history: Cold intolerance, constipation and dry skin
Slow onset over months
No orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
exam: Nonpitting periorbital edema, bradycardia and delayed reflexes
No elevated jugular venous pressure or S3 gallop
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4
imaging: Pericardial effusion possible but no pulmonary congestion

severity.mild: NYHA class I–II: symptoms only with more than ordinary activity; comfortable at rest, no congestion on exam, BNP mildly elevated
severity.moderate: NYHA class III: symptoms with ordinary activity such as walking one block; mild crackles, elevated jugular venous pressure, pitting edema, BNP moderately elevated
severity.severe: NYHA class IV: symptoms at rest; orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, extensive edema, hypoxemia, BNP markedly elevated
severity.critical: Cardiogenic shock or acute pulmonary edema: hypotension, cool extremities, altered mental status, lactate elevation, respiratory failure requiring support

red_flags.meaning: Cardiogenic shock; needs urgent hemodynamic support and intensive care

red_flags.finding: Severe respiratory distress with pink frothy sputum
red_flags.meaning: Acute pulmonary edema; needs urgent noninvasive ventilation or intubation
Hypoperfusion or hypoxemia; indicates critical illness

red_flags.finding: Chest pain with ischemic ECG changes or rising troponin
red_flags.meaning: Acute coronary syndrome as the precipitant; needs urgent reperfusion evaluation

red_flags.finding: New rapid atrial fibrillation or sustained ventricular arrhythmia
red_flags.meaning: Arrhythmia driving decompensation; needs rate or rhythm control and consideration of anticoagulation

red_flags.finding: Fever with productive cough or focal lung findings
red_flags.meaning: Pneumonia as a precipitant; needs antibiotics and may worsen heart failure

red_flags.finding: Rapid weight gain with worsening edema despite diuretics
red_flags.meaning: Worsening congestion; may need intravenous diuresis or medication adjustment

complications.name: Ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death
Pulmonary hypertension
clues: Elevated estimated pulmonary artery pressure on echocardiography

special_populations.differences: May present with confusion, falls, poor appetite or generalized weakness rather than classic dyspnea; symptoms are often attributed to aging. Polypharmacy and renal impairment increase the risk of medication-related decompensation.

Normal pregnancy causes mild dyspnea, leg swelling and fatigue, so worsening orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and a new murmur are the clues. Peripartum cardiomyopathy should be considered in the late third trimester or up to five months postpartum.

Volume overload from kidney disease can mimic heart failure; edema and dyspnea overlap and BNP is elevated by reduced clearance. Diuretic dosing and renin-angiotensin blockade require careful monitoring.
Autonomic neuropathy can blunt exertional symptoms, and patients may present later with silent ischemia or advanced congestion. Diabetes is a common driver and affects management.
Breathlessness and leg swelling are blamed on weight; edema may be hard to see and BNP can be lower than expected. Weight loss and sleep apnea treatment improve symptoms.

Heart failure in children is usually due to congenital heart disease or cardiomyopathy. Infants present with feeding difficulty, poor growth, sweating with feeds and tachypnea rather than classic orthopnea.

key_questions.question: What brings you in today — what has been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Exertional shortness of breath, fatigue, or leg swelling as the leading complaint

key_questions.question: How much can you do before you get short of breath? Has this changed from a month ago?
key_questions.looking_for: Declining exercise tolerance; helps assign NYHA functional class

key_questions.question: How many pillows do you sleep on? Can you lie flat?
key_questions.looking_for: Orthopnea — needing extra pillows or sleeping upright suggests pulmonary congestion

key_questions.question: Do you ever wake up at night gasping for air?
key_questions.looking_for: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, a classic congestion symptom

key_questions.question: Have your ankles, legs, or belly been swelling? Have your shoes or rings gotten tight?
key_questions.looking_for: Peripheral edema and abdominal distention from fluid retention

key_questions.question: Have you gained weight recently? How fast?
key_questions.looking_for: Rapid weight gain over days to weeks from fluid, not fat

key_questions.question: Do you get tired or winded with activities that used to be easy?
key_questions.looking_for: Fatigue and reduced functional capacity

key_questions.question: Do you have a cough, especially at night or when lying down? Any pink or frothy sputum?
key_questions.looking_for: Dry nocturnal cough; pink frothy sputum suggests acute pulmonary edema

key_questions.question: Do you have chest pain or pressure with exertion?
key_questions.looking_for: Ischemic symptoms suggesting coronary disease as the cause or trigger

key_questions.question: Have you had a heart attack, heart failure, or heart valve problem before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior cardiac disease that explains the current syndrome

key_questions.question: Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, kidney disease, or sleep apnea?
key_questions.looking_for: Common drivers and precipitants of heart failure

key_questions.question: Have you been taking your heart or blood pressure medications? Any recent changes?
key_questions.looking_for: Nonadherence or a stopped diuretic as the trigger for decompensation

key_questions.question: Do you take any anti-inflammatory pain relievers like ibuprofen or naproxen?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs cause sodium and water retention and can precipitate heart failure

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had heart failure, a cardiomyopathy, or sudden cardiac death at a young age?
key_questions.looking_for: Inherited cardiomyopathy or familial risk

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, drink alcohol, or use any recreational drugs?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco, heavy alcohol, or stimulant use as contributing causes

key_questions.question: Have you ever received chemotherapy or radiation to the chest?
key_questions.looking_for: Cardiotoxic exposure causing cardiomyopathy

key_questions.question: Any fever, chills, or recent infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Infection as a precipitant; fever argues for pneumonia or endocarditis

key_questions.question: Any palpitations or racing heartbeat?
key_questions.looking_for: Atrial fibrillation or other arrhythmia driving decompensation

key_questions.question: Any lightheadedness, fainting, or confusion?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypoperfusion or arrhythmia; syncope or altered mental status suggests severe disease

key_questions.question: Any pain, redness, or swelling in just one leg?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral findings suggest deep vein thrombosis rather than heart failure

reasoning_points: Exertional dyspnea with declining exercise tolerance is the cardinal symptom
Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea indicate pulmonary congestion
Bilateral pitting edema, weight gain, and abdominal bloating indicate systemic congestion
Elevated jugular venous pressure, an S3 gallop, and pulmonary crackles support the diagnosis on exam
An elevated BNP or NT-proBNP supports a cardiac cause of dyspnea
Echocardiography classifies the type (reduced vs preserved ejection fraction) and identifies the cause
A reversible precipitant should be sought: ischemia, arrhythmia, infection, nonadherence, NSAIDs, or anemia
Look-alikes such as COPD, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, nephrotic syndrome, and cirrhosis should be considered and excluded

easy: Older adult with known hypertension or prior myocardial infarction
Classic story of exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and ankle swelling
Elevated jugular venous pressure, crackles at the bases, and pitting edema on exam
Elevated BNP and reduced ejection fraction on echocardiography
medium: Older adult presenting with fatigue, poor appetite, or confusion rather than dyspnea
Obesity masking edema and blunting BNP elevation
Atrial fibrillation as the precipitant with an irregularly irregular pulse
Coexisting COPD making it hard to tell cardiac from pulmonary dyspnea
hard: Preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) with a normal or mildly elevated BNP
Renal impairment with volume overload and an elevated BNP from reduced clearance
Pregnancy with physiologic dyspnea and leg swelling, or peripartum cardiomyopathy
Cardiogenic shock with hypotension, cool extremities, and elevated lactate
Acute pulmonary edema with pink frothy sputum requiring urgent support
